sense: something one has undertaken to do; an engagement

terms.gloss: an engagement, business that keeps one occupied
evidence: Cic. Fam. 12.30.2: maximīs occupātiōnibus distinēbar (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Or. 34: in maximīs occupātiōnibus tuīs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “the usual meaning, esp. of public service”. Its first sense is the seizing of a place. The participle occupātus is “busy, tied up”.

phrases.english: I was kept from it by very heavy commitments

phrases.latin: itaque nēmō adhūc convenīre mē voluit, cui fuerim occupātus
phrases.english: and so no one who has wanted to see me has yet found me tied up

phrases.latin: Crās nōn possum: aliīs occupātiōnibus distineor.
phrases.english: I can’t tomorrow: I have other commitments.

sources: Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica), checked against the editions named there.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
The example sentences marked “composed” are ours.
